t.1.69.1: Śakuntalā said: O king, you see the faults of others, though they are only the size of mustard seeds, but your own, the size of bilva fruits, you do not see even while seeing them.
t.1.69.3: You roam upon the earth, O king, while I move through the sky. See the difference between us two, like that between Mount Meru and a mustard seed.
t.1.69.2: Menakā is counted among the Thirty Gods, and the Thirty Gods follow after Menakā; my birth, Duḥṣanta, surpasses your birth.
t.1.69.5: And true too is this saying which I shall tell you, O sinless one, for the sake of illustration and not out of malice; having heard it, you ought to forgive me.
t.1.69.4: I visit in turn the abodes of great Indra, of Kubera, of Yama, and of Varuṇa; behold my power, O king!
t.1.69.6: As long as an ugly man does not see his own face in a mirror, so long does he consider himself more handsome than others.
t.1.69.7: But when he looks upon his misshapen face in a mirror, then he realizes that it is he himself who is the other, and not the other person.
t.1.69.9: For a fool, hearing the words, both good and bad, of people who are talking, takes up only the bad speech, just as a pig picks out filth.
t.1.69.10: But the wise man, having heard the good and bad words of men who chatter, takes up the speech that has merit, as the haṃsa draws milk out of water.
t.1.69.8: One who is truly endowed with great beauty despises no one; but one who chatters on excessively with harsh words becomes a tormentor of others in this world.
t.1.69.11: Just as a good man is pained when he speaks ill of others, so a wicked man is pleased when he speaks ill of others.
t.1.69.12: Just as the good attain contentment by respectfully greeting their elders, so the fool becomes content by reviling a good man.
t.1.69.14: Nothing else in the world is more laughable than this: when a wicked man himself calls a good man wicked.
t.1.69.15: From a man who has fallen away from the dharma of truth, as from an angry venomous serpent, even an unbeliever shrinks in fear; how much more, then, a believer!
t.1.69.16: He who, having himself begotten a son resembling him, then scorns him, the gods destroy his fortune, and he does not attain the worlds.
t.1.69.17: For the ancestors have declared a son to be the foundation of family and lineage, the highest of all dharmas; therefore one should not abandon a son.
t.1.69.13: Fools who are blind to their own faults yet keep searching out the faults of others live happily; though they themselves deserve to be reproached by others, they call others such.
t.1.69.19: Sons, once born, bring men merit and renown and increase the joy of their hearts; serving as rafts of dharma, they rescue their fathers from hell.
t.1.69.20: Therefore you, tiger among kings, ought not to abandon your son, O lord of the earth, protecting yourself, truth and dharma; lion among men, you should not take on deceit here.
t.1.69.18: Manu declared five kinds of sons: those born of one's own wife, those obtained, those bought, those reared, and those adopted, as well as those begotten on other women.
t.1.69.21: Better than a hundred wells is a reservoir; better than a hundred reservoirs is a sacrifice; better than a hundred sacrifices is a son; and better than a hundred sons is truth.
t.1.69.22: A thousand horse sacrifices and truth were weighed in the balance, and truth alone outweighed the thousand horse sacrifices.
t.1.69.24: There is no dharma higher than truth, and nothing is found that is superior to truth; nor indeed is anything found here more grievous than falsehood.
t.1.69.23: Mastery of all the Vedas and bathing at all the sacred fords, and the truth of one who speaks it, O king, may be equal, or they may not be equal.
t.1.69.25: O king, truth is the supreme brahman, and truth is the highest covenant. Do not forsake your pledge, O king; let your union be true.
t.1.69.26: If your attachment is to falsehood, and if you yourself do not believe me, then alas, I shall go of my own accord; with one such as you there can be no union.
t.1.69.28: Having spoken these words, Śakuntalā set out to depart. Then a bodiless voice from the sky spoke to Duḥṣanta, who was at that time surrounded by his officiating priests, his family priest, his teachers and his ministers.
t.1.69.27: Even without you, Duḥṣanta, my son will rule and protect this four-cornered earth, which wears the king of mountains as its crest-ornament.
t.1.69.29: The mother is but a leather bag; the son belongs to the father, and the one by whom he is begotten is that very one. Support your son, Duḥṣanta, and do not scorn Śakuntalā.
t.1.69.31: A wife gives birth to a son who is a part of one's own self, divided in two. Therefore, O Duḥṣanta, O king, support your son, the child of Śakuntalā.
t.1.69.32: This is misfortune: who, while living, would abandon his own living son? Support the great-souled son of Śakuntalā, the son of Duḥṣanta, O Paurava!
t.1.69.30: A son, O god among men, lifts up the one who sowed the seed from the abode of Yama. You are the begetter of this child; Śakuntalā has spoken the truth.
t.1.69.34: Having heard that utterance of the heaven-dwellers, the Paurava king, greatly delighted, spoke these words to his family priest and his ministers.
t.1.69.33: Since this boy is to be supported by you, and that at our word as well, let this son of yours therefore be called by the name Bharata.
t.1.69.35: Let you, sirs, hear this speech of this divine messenger. I myself too know him to be just so, my own son.
t.1.69.36: If I were to accept this son of mine on her word alone, the people would surely harbor suspicion, and thus he would not be pure.
t.1.69.38: Smelling him on the head, he embraced him with affection; honored by the brahmins and praised by the bards, the king attained the supreme joy that is born from the touch of a son.
t.1.69.37: Then, O Bhārata, the king, having had him vindicated by the divine messenger, joyful and delighted, accepted him as his son.
t.1.69.39: The king, knower of dharma, honored that wife of his in accordance with dharma, and he spoke these words to her, first soothing her with gentle comfort.
t.1.69.40: This union with you was made out of the sight of the world; therefore, O queen, I deliberated on this for the sake of your purification.
t.1.69.43: Having spoken thus to her, his beloved queen, the royal sage Duḥṣanta honored her with garments, food and drink, O Bhārata.
t.1.69.41: For the people would think that your union with me came about merely from a woman's passion, and this son has been chosen by me for the kingship; that is why I weighed the matter thus.
t.1.69.42: And the unkind words that you, exceedingly angered, spoke to me, my dear, I have forgiven you, for you love me, O wide-eyed, lovely one.
t.1.69.44: And then King Duḥṣanta, having named his son, the son of Śakuntalā, Bharata, consecrated him at that time as heir apparent.
t.1.69.45: The famed wheel of that great-souled one rolled forth, radiant, divine, unconquered, mighty, making the worlds resound.
t.1.69.47: That king became a mighty universal sovereign, ruler of the whole earth, and he sacrificed with many sacrifices, just as Śakra, the lord of the Maruts.
t.1.69.46: Having conquered the kings of the earth, he made them subject to his will. He practiced the dharma of the good and attained unsurpassed fame.
t.1.69.49: From Bharata comes the fame of the Bhāratas, through whom this lineage is called Bhārata; and those who came later and those who came before are renowned as Bhāratas.
t.1.69.48: Kaṇva performed the sacrifice for him, as for Dakṣa, a king lavish with sacrificial fees; and that glorious one accomplished the horse sacrifice called Govitata, in which Bharata gave Kaṇva a thousand padmas.
t.1.69.50: For in the lineage of Bharata there arose many excellent kings, godlike and of great might, and like unto Brahman as well.
t.1.69.51: Of those whose names are altogether beyond measure, I shall recount to you, O Bhārata, the foremost ones, those greatly fortunate ones, like unto gods, devoted to truth and uprightness.
